title: How to Succeed in Academic Medicine: Publishing Strategy
subtitle: Some thoughts on how to win from somebody who hasn't really done that...
body_html:
Hi, I write a newsletter. I'm a relapsing and remitting researcher. I really hate writing science articles, because I'm basically not allowed to be funny. If there was a humor of satirically presented results and tongue-in-cheek findings, that would be a much more successful academic. Ironically, many of the early papers in the field of psychiatry have a level of wordsmithing and beautiful writing that we just don't see anymore.

And now, a plug for my upcoming event.

The Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment is May 18th, 2025, in Los Angeles.

It’s held at the swanky Skyline Loft at 224 East 11th Street #601 Los Angeles, CA 90015.

Get your RAMHT Tickets Now!

Yes, that is when the APA is in town.

The point of these events was to take a conceit—fast-paced discussions about treatments and tools that challenge our conceptions of what is possible in mental health care.

Our speakers include:

  • Grady Hannah, Co-Founder, Executive Team Member, Attentio AI, Co-Founder NightWare

  • Kellie Newsome, NP, co-host Carlat Psychiatry Podcast

  • Carlene MacMillan, M.D., DFAACAP, FCTMSS, Chief Product Officer at Radial

  • Daniel Karlin, M.D. Chief Medical Officer, MindMed

  • Jay Sanguinetti, Ph.D., Founder and President, Sanm.ai

  • Sandhya Prashad, M.D., Medical Director Houston Ketamine Therapeutics & Houston Deep TMS Therapy, President at American Society of Ketamine Physicians

  • David Carreon, M.D., Acacia Clinics

  • Sarah Norman, Executive Director, BrainFutures. Former CMS

  • Chris Aiken, M.D., Director, Psych Partners. Editor of The Carlat Report

  • Oded Kraft, Co-founder, CEO at GrayMatters Health

  • Dominik Middelmann, Co-Founder & CEO MDHub

  • Jonathan Seltzer, CEO SimplePractice

  • Jonathan Downar, MD, Co-Founder, Ampa Health

  • Chris Dougherty, Founder and Chief Strategist at Hydra Strategies

It is going to be lit. Now, to the article.

Just for a minute, here's a little bit of text from the DH Winnicott classic “Hate in the countertransference:”

Yes, a serious, even field-defining article includes a list of reason mothers hate their babies.

That's from 1949. The atomic bomb has already been dropped. We were in the modern age.

I'll quit complaining about the fact that I can't write linguistically fun stuff for academic journals, and get on with the point. Academic rating needs to be concise, humor, less so!

Academic journals still matter. To be clear, they're a scam. By a scam, I mean it's a huge industry that makes billions of dollars off of the work of physicians and other scientist are doing that work for free. Or, paying for the privilege.

Getting past that particular part of academic publishing, it's still an important part of the careers of many individuals, and it's one of the ways that we get new evidence in the world so that everybody can get their patients better.

I'm responsible for enough academic publications that it is very hard to keep track of them all. I'm not the most well cited researcher in the world, because I didn't really think about that as part of the game until was already in the thick of it.

The way academic work is measured is by citations. This is true for both the academic work itself and truth the journals that publish it. It's also true for the academics in question. Like anything that can get you a job, or lose your job, or to find your career, there's some gaming system that can happen.

Let's start with how the system works. When you write an academic article, it has four parts. It has an introduction, methods, results, discussion. There's also an abstract and a quick conclusion. There are pretty strict limits on how many words you can have in that article, and the more prestigious the journal, the less words you're likely to get.

In that academic article, in the introduction, you set up why you did your study or review. You're going to cite prior evidence:

Depression is bad [Citation]. Tradition traditional treatments aren't very good [citation]. We wanted to understand if this new treatment would be helpful in depression, which prior studies suggested be the possible [citation]. However, this is the first time…

When you're writing a paper, everything you say in the introduction that's a claim needs a citation. You can't just say depression is bad—you need to reference someone's prior research demonstrating that depression is bad. That paper now has its citation count go up by one. The more citations on a paper, the more impactful it is judged to be. Successful academic researchers have their work cited by other academics. Cranking out 100 papers that nobody cites is less important than cranking out one paper that 100 people cite, by an order of magnitude or more.

The way we recognize science is important is that it impacts the science of others.

It also lets you know that there's a popularity contest going on, because when you're writing a review article, or preparing your own original research, you're likely to read other people's articles, and you're looking at their citations. You might even cite their citations. Things with lots of citations get cited again, so there's a snowballing effect.

Thus, if you want to be a successful academic, you need to write works that's likely be interesting to other people, and worth citing.

As astute individuals may have already recognized there's a way to gain the system a little bit. What if you write 100 papers, and then you cite all of your prior papers every time you write a new paper?

Then your first paper would be cited 100 times, your second paper would be cited 99 times, et cetera.

One system for tracking impact is called the H-index, which is a measure of how important you are as a researcher. It has a pretty simple formula: in H-index of two means you have two papers, each cited twice. An H-index of three means you have three papers, each been cited three times.

It's a game-able system. Enter the i10 index—a product of Google, it turns out. They have a simpler system. You get one point for every paper that has 10 citations or more.

It also excludes self-citations, practically, so it's less easy to game in one way, at least.

Either way, if you're not thinking about the citation systems while you're writing a paper, you're likely to write papers that won’t get cited as much as would be beneficial for your career. Impactful research is interesting to other people. They're going to read it, and they're going to have a reason to cite it. If only a little bit of your career is your academic success, it pays to be aware of how that career is measured. It's not just “publish or perish,” it's publish and get cited, maybe even more than 10 times for a paper, and more quickly is better than less quickly.

One “back of the envelope” way to know if an academic is on track is to look at the number of years they've been working, and then look at the number of citations they have. An H-index Point per year is considered respectable.

I asked ChatGPT about this, and it cranked out this chart:

I'm not at tenure committee, so I'm not here to judge, but I can't tell you that as a clinical assistant professor, which puts me somewhere in mid-career, with an h-index of 7, I am mid. I am an acceptably cited mid career academic who isn't actually an academic for a living, thank goodness.

One of the reasons for this is that it's not actually my job, but another reason is I didn't think, earlier in my career, about writing research that would be interesting to other people. I thought about writing research that was interesting to me. I didn't do anything to make sure that research, especially if it came out as a poster, needed to later be published as a paper so that more people would see it. Who has the time! But also, most of my publishing has been around post marketing data. This is not the most exciting, new, impactful science, at least not yet. A nice review paper, that's likely to get cited more than post marketing papers, especially in less than flashy domains like transcranial magnetic stimulation! I wasn't publishing sexy science. I wasn't publishing broadly popular reviews. Thus, I decided to change that, and write some reviews that would be really useful to large audiences. And it's working! Look at the growth of my impactfulness…

What happened in 2024? Well, I wrote an entire series of reviews about psychedelic medicines. I wrote those reviews for an audience of primary care physicians. I wrote them with a series of co-authors, and I made sure they were easy to read. Those papers are now getting cited, frequently. Some of my research with other co-authors around transcranial magnetic stimulation also has taken off. It takes time for people to get to know what you're writing about. When you do more and more work in a specific area, other people doing work in that area are likely to look to your papers. If you're lucky, they even set up an alert on Google so that every time you publish something, they get to know about it. This increases the readership of your papers, and increases the likelihood that you're going to get cited. Psychedelic medicine is much more exciting than post marketing data on sub-groups of people with different versions of broad versus focused TMS coils. However, I could also have been better at writing more compelling articles on the topic I was interested in, and, crucially, written better titles.

The degree to which the title matters is just so hard to qualify accurately, but it's close to everything. That title needs to be clear, catchy, and it needs to be what other people will be searching for. You could have an earth shaking conclusion in an article, but if your title sucks, no one's ever going to read it. Title should be clear, descriptive, and not bury the lead.

Here's an example of a terrible title:

That paper was one of the earlier publications demonstrating that non-inferiority was likely in the context of comparison of accelerated versus not accelerated TMS with the deep H coil systems. It's a pretty big data to set for the time. I know, you are asleep already. How about:

“Accelerated dTMS in Five Days May be Effective in the Treatment of Major Depression: a review of exciting evidence"

…may have been a better title. I feel like it really buries the lead. Also, I should've taken that from a poster and just written it into a paper, and that would've been more popular.

My point? Titles matter, think about them, spend some time on them, pay attention to what works, pay attention to what you search for, and try to write your articles accordingly.

I asked some fancier colleagues, like Stanford-trained David Carreon, M.D., and he agreed with the sexy title… “you should want to spend…time with it!” he also highlighted the crucial importance of keeping your audience in mind when it comes to that first figure in the paper. The title, plus the first figure, may be the only things people see. The first figure needs to get a point across that's easy to understand in about one second. Good title, very easy to understand figure one? Now you're off to the races and people might even read your abstract. If Lucky, they'll read your paper.

People are busy, and not paying attention, and didn't spend five years on your clinical trial, or a year on your review paper, they've got one second to decide if it's worth their time. Leave them in no doubt.

I hope that's helpful article for my readers, and feel free to share it if you think that's the case.

Share
